definition: Interlocutor means a person who takes part in a dialogue or conversation.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word interlocutor. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know interlocutor should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A good oral exam needs a real interlocutor: the examiner asks, listens, and follows up, so the candidate is conversing rather than reciting.
An eavesdropper stops far short of an interlocutor, hiding outside the exchange it secretly follows.
An onlooker goes a step further than an eavesdropper — at least visible at the talk's edge — but still short of an interlocutor, who speaks and is answered.

A conversationalist is someone praised for skill at conversation — quick, warm, easy to talk with. Interlocutor praises nothing; it simply names the role of the person you are talking with. A dull mumbler can still be your interlocutor, but only a gifted talker earns conversationalist.

Your counterpart is the person across the table in talks — the opposite number holding your role on the other side, who may say nothing at all. An interlocutor is defined by exchange: the person actually conversing with you. Counterpart is a matter of position; interlocutor, of participation.

The chess columnist writes as though a skeptical interlocutor sat across the desk: every paragraph answers a question no one has asked aloud — 'But why not take the pawn?' — and the column reads like half of a very good conversation.
Interlocutor is the formal word for a person inside a conversation — the one you are talking with, not merely to.
An audience receives; a bystander overhears; an interlocutor answers back, and the exchange needs that second voice to exist.
Interlocutor appears in philosophy, diplomacy and linguistics: the person one converses with.
In everyday talk, say partner or simply 'the other person.' Counterpart fits negotiations; conversationalist praises skill.
Use interlocutor when the exchange itself is under discussion and the role needs a precise name.

Language apps taught me a thousand flashcards; my grandmother's rule taught me more.
Real fluency, she insisted, begins the day you find a regular interlocutor -- an actual person who answers back, mishears you, laughs, and makes you repair the wreckage in real time.
So every Thursday I call Senhora Alves, a retired pharmacist in Porto who corrects my past tense and does not care that my accent makes her wince.
She is not a teacher and claims no patience for grammar.
Her one job is to reply, which no flashcard has ever done.
After six months, the app still rates my vocabulary higher than my speech.
The Thursday calls say otherwise.
